plot: Second person, viral 'What Was Life REALLY Like' format: you live in Pompeii in 79 AD; ten chapters answer daily-life questions (home, street food and garum, water and toilets, fuller's urine laundry and Vespasian's tax, the amphitheatre and the AD 59 riot, wall graffiti, the chained guard dog, health and teeth, cool autumn nights), then the eruption, Pliny the Elder's real rescue and death at Stabiae and the next-morning surge; the gothic last chapter is the hollows in the ash (Fiorelli's casts) and the 2018 charcoal note that moves the date from August to about 24 October.

beats.say: Pompeii, 79 AD. You have one day left, and nobody knows.
Fresh bread! Hot from the oven! Get it before it's gone!
You cross a stone street toward the smell of bread.
Behind the town, a green mountain is quietly waking up.
So what was life really like here, before the end?
Your home, your food, your job, your fun. And your last morning.
Chapter one. Where do you live?
About eleven thousand people live in Pompeii, on the Bay of Naples.
If you're rich, you live in a house built around a courtyard.
Painted walls. A garden. A pool that catches rainwater from the roof.
The front hall is called the atrium. It's where guests wait.
Each morning, poorer men line up there to ask for favours.
Your house has almost no windows facing the street.
The street is loud, dirty and full of strangers. Keep it out.
But you probably aren't rich. Most people aren't.
So you rent one or two rooms above a shop.
No kitchen. No running water. Maybe one small window.
Wait. No kitchen? Then where do I eat?
Rich families eat dinner lying on couches, three to a couch.
Same place as everyone. Out on the street!
Chapter two. What do you eat?
Your day starts with bread. Pompeii has dozens of bakeries.
Round loaf, cut into eight. Tear off a piece and go.
Archaeologists found eighty-one of these loaves in one bakery oven.
They had turned to black charcoal. Still in their eight pieces.
Someone put them in to bake, and never came back.
For lunch, you go to a street counter. A Roman fast-food bar.
Lentils, sausage, hot wine! Sit or stand, your choice!
Big clay pots are sunk into the counter to keep food warm.
In 2020, diggers opened one of these bars. Fully painted.
Inside the pots were traces of duck, pig, goat, fish and snails.
And a painted dog on a leash, right on the counter.
One bar wall even lists the wine prices.
One coin, wine. Two, the best. Four, the famous Falernian.
And on almost everything, you pour garum.
Fish sauce! Fish guts, salted and left in the sun for weeks.
That's disgusting. Can I have some more?
One rich man in Pompeii got rich selling exactly that sauce.
His house floor shows garum jars, made in mosaic.
And the fruit stalls today? Pomegranates. Chestnuts. Walnuts.
Remember those. They matter at the very end.
Chapter three. Where do you get water? And where's the toilet?
An aqueduct brings fresh mountain water all the way to town.
It flows through lead pipes to fountains on the street corners.
There are about forty of them. You carry water home in jars.
The water never stops. It runs day and night, into the street.
Look down. The streets have big stepping stones across them.
Because the street carries rainwater, mud and worse. Much worse.
Cart wheels wore deep grooves into the stone, still there today.
Your toilet? In many houses, it's in the kitchen. By the stove.
Next to the food? Who thought that was a good idea?
The drain is there. Makes sense to me!
Or a public toilet. A long stone bench. No walls. No privacy.
Then you go to the baths. Almost everyone does, every afternoon.
Warm room, hot room, cold pool. For one small coin.
The Stabian Baths are the oldest in town. They still stand.
Chapter four. What's your job?
Many people in Pompeii are enslaved. They do the hardest work.
Free people run shops, bakeries, bars, and workshops.
Shops open straight onto the street. At night, wooden shutters slide shut.
You want work? I clean clothes. Grab a pot.
He's a fuller. A laundry worker. And his secret soap?
Urine. Pots stand on street corners for people to fill.
It lifts out grease and stains. Best cleaner there is!
You stomp on wet clothes in a tub, all day. Barefoot.
Rome even taxed urine. The emperor Vespasian brought in that tax.
His son complained. Vespasian held up a coin. Does it stink?
Money doesn't stink. People still say that today.
Vespasian died in June of 79. His son Titus now rules.
Titus has no idea what's about to happen on his watch.
Chapter five. What do you do for fun?
You go to the amphitheatre. Pompeii's is the oldest stone one left.
Around twenty thousand seats. Bigger than the whole town's population.
People come from nearby towns to watch gladiators fight.
Just don't sit near the fans from Nuceria.
Gladiators are celebrities. Fans scratch their names into the walls.
One wall calls a gladiator named Celadus the heartthrob of the girls.
Pompeii also has two theatres, for plays, music and comedy.
Twenty years ago, a fight in the stands became a riot.
Rome was so angry, it banned games here for ten years.
Someone even painted the riot on a wall, like a news photo.
And the walls talk. There is writing everywhere in Pompeii.
Election posters in big red letters. Vote for this man!
Love notes. Insults. Sums of money. Who owes who.
One person scratched a joke that appears again and again.
Wall, I'm amazed you haven't collapsed, holding up all this boring writing.
Two thousand years old, and it's still funny.
Chapter six. Who are your gods?
Every home has a small shrine, painted on the wall.
Painted snakes guard it. Snakes here mean luck and protection.
Every day, your family leaves a little food or wine there.
In town there are temples to Jupiter, Apollo, Venus, and Isis.
Isis was an Egyptian goddess. Her temple was rebuilt after the earthquake.
An inscription says a six-year-old boy paid to rebuild it.
Really, his rich father paid. It bought the family power.
Because in Pompeii, power means elections. Every single year.
But only free men can vote. Women can't. Enslaved people can't.
Women still paint posters, though. Backing the man they want to win.
Chapter seven. How safe are you?
At one front door, a black mosaic dog. Cave canem.
It means beware of the dog. Homes still use those words today.
Guard dogs were real. Chained by the front door, day and night.
In 1874, diggers found one of those dogs. Still on its chain.
Its owners had fled. Nobody came back to unclip it.
So the next time you see beware of the dog, remember Pompeii.
And thieves? Rich homes had strongboxes bolted to the floor.
At night the streets are pitch black. You carry an oil lamp.
But the real danger is under your feet.
Seventeen years ago, a huge earthquake wrecked this town.
They're still repairing it. Scaffolding, cracked walls, half-built temples.
And for days now, the ground has been shivering again.
Little shakes. That's Campania. You get used to them.
Nobody here knows Vesuvius is a volcano. It's covered in vineyards.
One painting shows the wine god standing in front of it. Smiling.
Chapter eight. What if you get sick?
You visit a doctor. One house here had dozens of surgical tools.
Probes, hooks, forceps. Some look almost like the ones used today.
No painkillers like ours. Maybe some wine first. And luck.
But here's a surprise. Your teeth are probably great.
Scans of victims found healthy teeth. Their food had very little sugar.
Bread, beans, fruit, fish. A diet many doctors would like today.
Still, life is short. Many children don't live to grow up.
Chapter nine. Are you warm when you sleep?
This morning is cool. People wear wool cloaks.
At home, you warm your hands over a brazier of glowing coals.
Your bedroom is tiny and dark. A bed, a lamp, a chest.
Outside, carts rattle past on the stones before sunrise.
Inns near the town gates rent beds to travellers and their mules.
It's noisy, it's crowded, and it smells. And you love it here.
And remember the fruit? Pomegranates, chestnuts. Cool mornings. Braziers.
Does that sound like the middle of summer to you?
Chapter ten. Your last day.
Ovens are full. Market's busy. A good day!
You wake up, grab bread, and fill your jar at the fountain.
The fruit sellers shout. A cart rattles past. A dog barks.
The ground shivers again. A little stronger this time.
There it goes again. Pass me that tray.
Nobody leaves. Why would they? It's just another busy morning.
Around one in the afternoon, the sky tears open.
The top of Vesuvius blows apart. A grey column shoots upward.
Over thirty kilometres high. Higher than any cloud you've seen.
Across the bay, a teenager named Pliny watches it rise.
He later writes that it looked like a giant pine tree.
What is that? Is the mountain on fire?
The wind carries the cloud straight over Pompeii. The sun goes out.
Then it starts raining stones. Light, grey, full of holes. Pumice.
They pile up fast. About fifteen centimetres every hour.
Inside! Everyone, under a roof! Now!
But roofs weren't built for that weight. Some start to give way.
So what do you do? Hide inside, or run?
Most people run. Experts think most of Pompeii got out in time.
My ovens are full. I'm not leaving my bread.
Some stay. To guard their homes. Or because they can't leave.
Five kilometres south, in Stabiae, warships arrive in the dark.
The admiral of the Roman fleet has come himself. Pliny the Elder.
He came to study the cloud. Then a friend begged for rescue.
His helmsman wanted to turn back. Pliny refused.
Fortune favours the brave. Steer for Pomponianus.
At his friend's villa, he took a bath and ate dinner.
Calmly. On purpose. So everyone else would stop panicking.
The mountain glowed with fire. He said it was burning farmhouses.
Then he went to bed, and snored loudly enough to hear outside.
By night, ash and stones nearly blocked his bedroom door.
They woke him. The house shook. Inside or out?
They went out, with pillows tied to their heads against the stones.
Morning came. But it was darker than any night.
On the shore, the sea was too wild to escape.
Pliny lay down, asking for cold water. Then a smell of sulphur.
He stood up, leaning on two men, and collapsed.
His nephew believed the fumes choked him. He was fifty-five.
Days later, his body was found unhurt. As if he were asleep.
And back in Pompeii, the worst had not even started.
Many who hid indoors had lived through the whole night of stones.
Then, early next morning, the giant column of smoke collapsed.
A cloud of burning gas and ash raced down the mountain.
Faster than a car. Nobody can outrun it.
Scientists call it a pyroclastic surge. It reached Pompeii in minutes.
Everyone still in town was gone in moments.
Then the ash kept falling, until the town disappeared.
Along the coast, the town of Herculaneum was buried even deeper.
In some places, under twenty metres of volcanic rock.
In its boathouses by the beach, about three hundred people waited.
Waiting for boats that never came. Diggers found them in the 1980s.
Families, close together, still facing the sea.
Chapter eleven. The town under the ash.
Pompeii stayed buried for almost seventeen hundred years.
Farmers planted vines on top of it. Nobody knew.
Diggers found it again in 1748. Then came the strangest discovery.
In the hardened ash, they kept finding empty spaces.
Hollows. And the hollows had shapes.
Shapes of people. Of hands. Of folds in a cloak.
The ash had hardened around the victims. Over time, they were gone.
Only the shape of their last moment stayed behind.
In 1863, an archaeologist named Giuseppe Fiorelli had an idea.
He poured liquid plaster into the hollows and waited.
When it set, they dug it out. Pompeii's people came back.
You can still stand next to them today.
Some are curled up. Some cover their faces. Some hold each other.
In 2024, DNA tests surprised everyone about who some of them were.
A famous 'mother and child' pair included an unrelated adult man.
The stories we told about them were our stories, not theirs.
More than eleven hundred victims have been found at Pompeii so far.
But one mystery stayed hidden for almost two thousand years.
The date. Every textbook said the twenty-fourth of August.
That date comes from Pliny's letters, copied by hand for centuries.
But remember the market? Pomegranates. Chestnuts. Walnuts.
Wool cloaks. Braziers burning. New wine already sealed in jars.
That's autumn, not August. Archaeologists noticed it too.
Then, in 2018, they found writing on a wall. In charcoal.
In a house being repaired, someone had scribbled a date.
The sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.
In our calendar, that's the seventeenth of October.
Charcoal fades fast. So it was likely written that same year.
Many historians now place the eruption around the twenty-fourth of October.
One copying slip may have moved the date by two months.
And the clue was sitting in a fruit basket the whole time.
So, could you have lived here? Fresh bread, hot baths, loud arenas?
The ground warned them for days. Listen to the small warnings.
Fresh bread! Hot from the oven! Get it before it's gone!
Would you run that morning, or stay home? Tell me below.

long.title: What Was Life REALLY Like in Pompeii, 79 AD?
long.description:
Would you have run that morning, or stayed with your home? Tell me in the comments.
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/gNlnRF0JtHY

Your home, your food, your job, your fun, and your last day in Pompeii, 79 AD. Street-food bars with duck and snails, fish sauce on everything, laundry washed in urine, a 20,000-seat arena, a guard dog still on its chain, and a mountain nobody knew was a volcano. Then the eruption, Pliny the Elder's rescue at Stabiae, the hollows in the ash, and a 2018 charcoal note that suggests the date in your textbook is two months off.

es.title: ¿Cómo era REALMENTE la vida en Pompeya en el 79 d. C.?
es.description:
¿Habrías huido esa mañana o te habrías quedado en casa? Cuéntamelo en los comentarios.

Tu casa, tu comida, tu trabajo, tu diversión y tu último día en Pompeya, año 79: bares callejeros con pato y caracoles, salsa de pescado en todo, ropa lavada con orina, un anfiteatro de 20.000 asientos, un perro guardián aún encadenado y una montaña que nadie sabía que era un volcán. Luego la erupción, el rescate de Plinio el Viejo, los huecos en la ceniza y una nota a carboncillo de 2018 que cambia la fecha.

pt.title: Como era REALMENTE a vida em Pompeia em 79 d.C.?
pt.description:
Você teria fugido naquela manhã ou ficado em casa? Conte nos comentários.

Sua casa, sua comida, seu trabalho, sua diversão e seu último dia em Pompeia, ano 79: bares de rua com pato e caracóis, molho de peixe em tudo, roupa lavada com urina, uma arena de 20 mil lugares, um cão de guarda ainda acorrentado e uma montanha que ninguém sabia ser um vulcão. Depois a erupção, o resgate de Plínio, o Velho, os vazios nas cinzas e uma inscrição a carvão de 2018 que muda a data.

ar.title: كيف كانت الحياة حقًا في بومبي عام 79م؟
ar.description:
هل كنت ستهرب ذلك الصباح أم تبقى في بيتك؟ أخبرني في التعليقات.

بيتك وطعامك وعملك ولهوك ويومك الأخير في بومبي عام 79: حانات شارع تقدّم البط والحلزون، صلصة السمك على كل شيء، ملابس تُغسل بالبول، مدرج يتسع لعشرين ألفًا، كلب حراسة ما زال مقيّدًا، وجبل لم يعرف أحد أنه بركان. ثم الثوران، ومحاولة إنقاذ بلينيوس الأكبر، والفراغات في الرماد، وكتابة بالفحم من 2018 تغيّر التاريخ.

fr.title: À quoi ressemblait VRAIMENT la vie à Pompéi en 79 ?
fr.description:
Auriez-vous fui ce matin-là ou seriez-vous resté chez vous ? Dites-le-moi en commentaire.

Votre maison, vos repas, votre travail, vos loisirs et votre dernier jour à Pompéi, en 79 : des comptoirs de rue avec canard et escargots, de la sauce de poisson partout, du linge lavé à l'urine, une arène de 20 000 places, un chien de garde encore enchaîné et une montagne que personne ne savait volcan. Puis l'éruption, le sauvetage de Pline l'Ancien, les creux dans la cendre et une inscription au charbon de 2018 qui change la date.

ja.title: 西暦79年ポンペイの暮らしは本当はどうだった?
ja.description:
あの朝、あなたなら逃げた?それとも家に残った?コメントで教えてください。

西暦79年ポンペイでのあなたの家、食事、仕事、娯楽、そして最後の一日。アヒルやカタツムリを出す屋台、何にでもかける魚醤、尿で洗う洗濯、2万席の円形闘技場、鎖につながれたままの番犬、そして誰も火山だと知らなかった山。噴火、大プリニウスの救助、灰の中の空洞、そして日付を覆す2018年の木炭の落書き。

ko.title: 서기 79년 폼페이의 삶은 정말 어땠을까?
ko.description:
그날 아침 당신이라면 도망쳤을까요, 집에 남았을까요? 댓글로 알려주세요.

서기 79년 폼페이에서의 집, 음식, 일, 놀이, 그리고 마지막 하루. 오리와 달팽이를 파는 길거리 가게, 모든 음식에 뿌리는 생선 소스, 소변으로 하는 빨래, 2만 석 원형경기장, 아직 사슬에 묶인 경비견, 아무도 화산인 줄 몰랐던 산. 그리고 분화, 대 플리니우스의 구조, 화산재 속 빈 공간, 날짜를 뒤집은 2018년 숯 낙서.

de.title: Wie war das Leben in Pompeji 79 n. Chr. WIRKLICH?
de.description:
Wärst du an diesem Morgen geflohen oder zu Hause geblieben? Schreib es in die Kommentare.

Dein Zuhause, dein Essen, deine Arbeit, dein Vergnügen und dein letzter Tag in Pompeji, 79 n. Chr.: Straßenimbisse mit Ente und Schnecken, Fischsoße auf allem, Wäsche mit Urin gewaschen, eine Arena mit 20.000 Plätzen, ein Wachhund noch an der Kette und ein Berg, den niemand für einen Vulkan hielt. Dann der Ausbruch, Plinius' Rettungsfahrt, die Hohlräume in der Asche und eine Kohleinschrift von 2018, die das Datum verschiebt.
